questions.question: Can general lower bounds be established for the circuit depth required to construct quantum expanders?
questions.quote: Such constructions exist using a variety of combinatorial tricks , but it has been an open question to provide general lower bounds on the depth.
questions.context: The paper constructs a constant-degree, constant-gap quantum expander on $n$ qubits using a depth-1 1D circuit, but whether general depth lower bounds exist for quantum expanders remains unknown.
questions.background: Understanding of quantum expander definitions, unitary circuit design, and lower bound techniques in quantum circuit complexity.
questions.title: Depth-1 expanders on the unitary group and applications

questions.question: Can streaming protocols be constructed to test closeness to ground states of translation-invariant 1D Hamiltonians using logarithmic memory?
questions.quote: It would be interesting to test for more natural states like ground states of translation-invariant Hamiltonians.
questions.context: The authors present a streaming protocol with logarithmic memory for testing closeness to a class of 1D volume-law entangled states, leaving open the extension to natural physical states such as ground states of translation-invariant Hamiltonians.
questions.background: Knowledge of quantum streaming algorithms, quantum state property testing, and 1D translation-invariant local Hamiltonians.
questions.title: Depth-1 expanders on the unitary group and applications

questions.question: Does there exist a 1D local Hamiltonian with a spectral gap of $\Omega(1/n)$ whose ground state is close to the CAT state?
questions.quote: Though the bound is nearly tight, we do not know of a local Hamiltonian with a ground state that is close to the CAT state itself and a spectral gap $\Omega(1/n)$ .
questions.context: The paper proves tight bounds relating spectral gap and entanglement, but constructing a local Hamiltonian with an $\Omega(1/n)$ spectral gap that has a ground state close to the CAT state remains open.
questions.background: Familiarity with 1D local Hamiltonians, spectral gap analysis, and CAT/GHZ state constructions.
questions.title: Depth-1 expanders on the unitary group and applications

questions.question: Is there a simpler proof for the spectral bound on the tensor representation $P\mapsto P^{\otimes 2}$ needed to build the unitary expander?
questions.quote: Thus, Theorem 2.3 is stronger than necessary for Theorem 2.13 , and we do not know whether the required bound for $P\mapsto P^{\otimes 2}$ admits a simpler proof.
questions.context: The paper derives a general representation-theoretic bound for $\mathrm{SL}(n;\mathbb{F}_2)$ to construct the expander, which is stronger than needed for the specific tensor representation $P\mapsto P^{\otimes 2}$.
questions.background: Representation theory of finite groups of Lie type such as $\mathrm{SL}(n;\mathbb{F}_2)$ and spectral gaps of quantum expanders.
questions.title: Depth-1 expanders on the unitary group and applications

questions.question: How can mechanism design for AI agents with unknown capabilities and alignment achieve full implementability (ensuring all equilibria yield the target outcome) to eliminate unwanted equilibria and deter agent collusion?
questions.quote: This is by no means the only solution concept—we expect that future work will tackle full implementability that could, among other things, deter collusion among agents.
questions.context: The paper establishes partial implementability, showing that the desired policy can be sustained as an equilibrium under direct mechanisms. However, it does not rule out alternative undesirable equilibria or collusion between agents.
questions.background: Familiarity with classical full implementation theory, Bayesian mechanism design, and collusion-proof equilibrium concepts.
questions.title: Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control

questions.question: What is the optimal reward coupling scheme across multiple AI agents, and how do such multi-agent incentive coupling principles scale to complex environments?
questions.quote: We think an interesting open problem is how reward should be optimally coupled then—and more broadly whether such principles might scale to more complicated environments.
questions.context: The paper presents stylized examples showing that coupling rewards can induce competition among multiple AI agents, but leaves open the systematic formulation of optimal reward coupling structures and their scalability.
questions.background: Understanding of contract theory, reward shaping, and multi-agent mechanism design.
questions.title: Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control

questions.question: Does every general instance of mixed manna under additive valuations admit an allocation that is simultaneously weighted envy-free up to one item (WEF1) and Pareto optimal (PO)?
questions.quote: First, does every general mixed manna instance admit a WEF1 and PO allocation? This remains open in the setting with equal entitlements .
questions.context: The paper proves that a complete WEF1 allocation always exists for arbitrary positive entitlements and additive valuations, but leaves open whether envy-freeness up to one item can be achieved simultaneously with Pareto optimality (PO), even in the unweighted (equal entitlement) setting.
questions.background: Familiarity with fair division concepts such as envy-freeness up to one item (EF1/WEF1) and Pareto optimality in discrete asset allocation.
questions.title: Weighted Fair Division of Indivisible Mixed Manna

questions.question: Which broader classes of additive mixed valuations beyond equal-magnitude valuations ($\{-a_i, 0, a_i\}$) admit exact weighted maximin share (WMMS) allocations under arbitrary entitlements or preserve an additive WMMS guarantee for WEF1 allocations?
questions.quote: Second, it would be useful to identify broader mixed valuation classes that admit exact WMMS under arbitrary entitlements, or in which WEF1 implies a meaningful additive WMMS guarantee.
questions.context: The paper establishes that exact WMMS allocations exist and are polynomial-time computable when agents have equal-magnitude valuations (values in $\{-a_i, 0, a_i\}$), but shows that adding a second positive valuation magnitude can destroy exact WMMS existence.
questions.background: Understanding of maximin share (MMS/WMMS) definitions, fair division algorithms, and valuation structures in discrete asset allocation.
questions.title: Weighted Fair Division of Indivisible Mixed Manna

questions.question: Can space-filling-curve-based surrogate metrics be constructed to approximate general $p$-Wasserstein distances $W_p$ between persistence diagrams for $1 \leq p < 2$?
questions.quote: A natural direction for future work is therefore to develop space-filling-curve-based surrogates for $W_{p}$ , with $1\leq p$
questions.context: The paper develops the Sierpiński--Knopp Wasserstein distance $d_{\mathrm{SK}}$ and surrogate $W_{\Gamma}$ specifically aimed at approximating the $2$-Wasserstein distance $W_2$ on persistence diagrams, leaving open how to construct analogous efficient space-filling curve surrogates for $p$-Wasserstein distances with $1 \leq p < 2$.
questions.background: Understanding of topological data analysis, optimal transport metrics $W_p$ on persistence diagrams, and space-filling curve encodings.
questions.title: Sierpiński--Knopp Wasserstein Distance for Persistence Diagrams and Applications to 2-Wasserstein Approximation

questions.question: How can normalization protocols for the Sierpiński--Knopp Wasserstein distance $d_{\mathrm{SK}}$ be adapted for online and iterative diagram settings?
questions.quote: Future work will investigate normalization protocols for online and iterative settings, space-filling-curve-based surrogates for the potentially more outlier-robust distances $W_{p}$ , $1\leq p$
questions.context: The proposed $d_{\mathrm{SK}}$ distance assumes a static normalization of persistence diagrams to the upper diagonal triangle of the unit square, but leaves unaddressed how to update or handle normalization when diagrams arrive dynamically in online or iterative computing pipelines.
questions.background: Familiarity with online algorithms and dynamic data structures in topological data analysis.
questions.title: Sierpiński--Knopp Wasserstein Distance for Persistence Diagrams and Applications to 2-Wasserstein Approximation

questions.question: Extend the cell decomposition framework for $k$-visibility queries from 2D polygons to 3D polyhedral environments.
questions.quote: Extending this cell decomposition paradigm to 3D polyhedral environments or investigating dynamic settings where polygon vertices are allowed to move present compelling challenges for future research in higher-order visibility.
questions.context: The paper provides a spatial cell decomposition of $\Theta(n^4)$ cells for 2D polygons (including polygons with holes) to answer $k$-visibility queries in $O(\log n + m)$ time. However, it does not characterize the geometric event surfaces or dynamic cell structures required for 3D polyhedral environments.
questions.background: Requires expertise in 3D visibility arrangements, polyhedral geometry, and spatial cell decomposition techniques.
questions.title: Efficient K-Visibility Query in Polygons

questions.question: Maintain and query $k$-visibility structures in dynamic settings where the vertices of the polygon are allowed to move.
questions.quote: Extending this cell decomposition paradigm to 3D polyhedral environments or investigating dynamic settings where polygon vertices are allowed to move present compelling challenges for future research in higher-order visibility.
questions.context: The paper establishes a static spatial partition of $\Theta(n^4)$ cells with a $\delta$-compression scheme for fixed polygons, but does not address dynamic updates or topological mutation events when polygon vertices move over time.
questions.background: Requires familiarity with kinetic data structures, dynamic geometry, and topological event maintenance in visibility arrangements.
questions.title: Efficient K-Visibility Query in Polygons

questions.question: Does $2$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion parameterized by the solution size $k$ admit a polynomial kernel on general graphs?
questions.quote: However, despite this progress, it remains open whether the problem admits a polynomial size kernel on general graphs.
questions.context: The paper establishes a polynomial vertex kernel of size $\mathcal{O}(k^5)$ for $2$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion restricted to interval graphs, but whether a polynomial kernel exists for general graphs without restriction remains unresolved.
questions.background: Familiarity with kernelization lower bound techniques (such as cross-composition) and structural parameterizations for graph modification problems.
questions.title: Kernelization of 2-Club Cluster Edge Deletion on Interval Graphs

questions.question: Is the $2$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion problem NP-hard on interval graphs?
questions.quote: In particular, it remains open whether the problem is NP-hard on interval graphs.
questions.context: The paper shows that $s$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion is solvable in polynomial time on unit interval graphs and NP-hard on split graphs, but the exact computational complexity of $2$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion on general interval graphs remains open.
questions.background: Understanding of NP-hardness reductions on graph classes and interval graph intersection representations.
questions.title: Kernelization of 2-Club Cluster Edge Deletion on Interval Graphs

questions.question: Can Reduction Rule 11 used in the kernelization of $2$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion on interval graphs be extended to $s$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion for arbitrary $s > 2$?
questions.quote: Consequently, extending Reduction Rule 11 to arbitrary $s$ remains an open problem and appears to require new structural insights.
questions.context: The paper develops structural reduction rules, specifically Reduction Rule 11, to obtain a polynomial kernel for $2$-Club Cluster Edge Deletion on interval graphs, but these rules do not immediately generalize to components of diameter $s > 2$.
questions.background: Knowledge of structural properties of $s$-clubs in interval graphs and data reduction rules in parameterized complexity.
questions.title: Kernelization of 2-Club Cluster Edge Deletion on Interval Graphs

questions.question: Can logarithmic or faster regret bounds be established for prediction-assisted LLM pricing and admission under structural assumptions such as second-order growth in demand or dual solution stability?
questions.quote: Stronger rates are possible under structural conditions on demand, second-order growth, or stable dual solutions.
questions.context: The paper proves a regret bound of $\widetilde O\left( \sqrt{T}+(1+\bar{\Lambda}) \min\{T\varepsilon,\sqrt{JT}\} \right)$ for Prediction-Clipped UCB without assuming margins between products or dual stability. It leaves open whether logarithmic regret can be proven under stronger structural conditions.
questions.background: Familiarity with online convex optimization, bandits with knapsacks (BwK), and margin or curvature conditions used to obtain logarithmic regret bounds.
questions.title: Prediction-Assisted Pricing and Admission for LLM APIs with Stochastic Token Consumption

questions.question: What is the maximum stable chromatic number $\chi_\mathrm{stable}(G)$ over all planar graphs $G$?
questions.quote: Determining the stable chromatic number of planar graphs remains open.
questions.context: The authors introduce the stable chromatic number $\chi_\mathrm{stable}(G)$ and prove general upper bounds based on treewidth ($O(t \log (1 + n/t))$) and acyclic orientations, but leave the precise maximum stable chromatic number of planar graphs open.
questions.background: Understanding of planar graph theory, standard graph coloring bounds, and the definition of stable graph coloring.
questions.title: Graph Coloring with Color Preferences

questions.question: What are tight upper and lower bounds on the stable chromatic number $\chi_\mathrm{stable}(G)$ for interval graphs?
questions.quote: Studying other graph classes, such as interval graphs, will also be fruitful.
questions.context: While general bounds on $\chi_\mathrm{stable}(G)$ are derived using treewidth and Grundy numbers, the authors do not determine tight bounds for restricted graph classes such as interval graphs.
questions.background: Familiarity with interval graphs, standard chromatic parameters, and graph preferences.
questions.title: Graph Coloring with Color Preferences

questions.question: What is the exact computational complexity of computing sparse coarse correlated equilibria (CCEs) in discounted general-sum Markov games, closing the gap between the quasi-polynomial upper bound and the lower bound under $\mathsf{ETH}$ for $\mathsf{PPAD}$?
questions.quote: First, a gap remains between our quasi-polynomial upper bounds and the computational lower bounds established in this paper; determining the precise complexity of computing sparse CCEs in discounted Markov games remains an important open problem.
questions.context: The paper proves that under $\mathsf{ETH}$ for $\mathsf{PPAD}$, computing inverse-polynomially accurate CCEs in discounted general-sum Markov games has no polynomial-time algorithm, and provides a quasi-polynomial-time radically uncoupled learning algorithm. It leaves open the exact complexity bound between these two frontiers.
questions.background: Familiarity with $\mathsf{PPAD}$-hardness, the Exponential Time Hypothesis for $\mathsf{PPAD}$, and equilibrium computation in Markov games.
questions.title: Independent Reinforcement Learning in Discounted Markov Games

questions.question: Do polynomial-time radically uncoupled online-learning algorithms exist for general-sum Markov games when players are restricted to Markov policies rather than general history-dependent policies?
questions.quote: Second, it would be interesting to determine whether polynomial-time radically uncoupled online-learning algorithms exist for general-sum Markov games when the considered policy classes for the players are restricted to Markov policies rather than general history-dependent policies.
questions.context: The authors develop a layered optimistic mirror descent algorithm with sub-exponential convergence for history-dependent policies in general-sum Markov games, but whether polynomial-time convergence is achievable under the restriction to Markov policies remains open.
questions.background: Knowledge of online mirror descent, Markov decision processes, and uncoupled learning dynamics in multi-agent reinforcement learning.
questions.title: Independent Reinforcement Learning in Discounted Markov Games

questions.question: Can information structures strictly weaker than shared randomness facilitate tractable (polynomial or quasi-polynomial time) uncoupled learning algorithms for equilibria in discounted general-sum Markov games?
questions.quote: In particular, it would be interesting to investigate whether information models weaker than shared randomness also make tractable algorithms possible.
questions.context: The paper analyzes learning guarantees under a radically uncoupled information model without shared randomness, but the theoretical boundary separating radically uncoupled settings from models with partial or full shared randomness remains uncharacterized.
questions.background: Understanding of communication models, uncoupled learning dynamics, and correlated equilibrium concepts in multi-agent systems.
questions.title: Independent Reinforcement Learning in Discounted Markov Games

questions.question: Can an exact closed-form formulation for the combinatorial function $s_*(n)$ be determined to precisely characterize the OBDD width for computing the middle bit of integer multiplication $\text{SMul}_{n-1}^n$ on a restricted domain?
questions.quote: First, we established only asymptotic bounds on $s_{*}(n)$ rather than an exact closed-form formulation, leaving its precise determination for future research.
questions.context: The paper proves that the OBDD width for computing $\text{SMul}_{n-1}^n$ on a restricted domain is $\Theta(2^{s_*(n)})$, but only establishes asymptotic bounds for $s_*(n)$ rather than an exact formula.
questions.background: Knowledge of ordered binary decision diagram (OBDD) lower bounds and combinatorial techniques for analyzing integer multiplication functions.
questions.title: Upper and lower bounds on the OBDD-width of a special integer multiplication

questions.question: Can the unification of upper and lower OBDD width bounds via combinatorial characterization for middle-bit integer multiplication $\text{SMul}_{n-1}^n$ be extended from a restricted input domain to arbitrary $n$-bit binary strings?
questions.quote: Furthermore, our unification is established only for a restricted class of $x$ and $y$ ; extending these results to arbitrary $n$ -bit binary strings presents a significantly more challenging problem.
questions.context: The paper unifies upper and lower OBDD width bounds for $\text{SMul}_{n-1}^n$, but this unification is restricted to inputs $x$ and $y$ drawn from a specific domain rather than arbitrary $n$-bit binary strings.
questions.background: Familiarity with OBDD complexity techniques and the structure of integer multiplication Boolean functions on general domain inputs.
questions.title: Upper and lower bounds on the OBDD-width of a special integer multiplication

questions.question: How can policy-gradient test-time updates in imperfect-information games be made persistent across playthroughs without corrupting or degrading the agent's global strategy?
questions.quote: This highlights a potential for future research that would enable persistent local updates, allowing agents to retain test-time insights across playthroughs without degrading global strategy.
questions.context: The paper shows that test-time policy-gradient updates enhance strategy quality, but because parameters are shared across the policy neural network, weights must currently be reset after each playthrough to prevent corrupting the global blueprint strategy.
questions.background: Understanding of policy-gradient algorithms, neural network function approximation, and subgame search in imperfect-information games.
questions.title: Test-time Reinforcement Learning in Imperfect Information Games

questions.question: How can test-time policy-gradient search in imperfect-information games be combined with depth-limited subgame solving and approximate value functions to enable faster gradient updates in long games?
questions.quote: Another promising direction is to combine our approach with depth-limited solving to allow faster gradient updates in long games.
questions.context: The authors introduce a test-time policy-gradient reasoning framework via implicit gadget games, but deliberately omit depth-limited search and value function approximations to isolate test-time reasoning effects from value approximation noise.
questions.background: Knowledge of imperfect-information value functions, depth-limited search methods, and policy-gradient reinforcement learning.
questions.title: Test-time Reinforcement Learning in Imperfect Information Games

questions.question: Which finite-variable logical fragments admit direct polynomial-time unlabeled model counting (UFOMC), rather than relying on a reduction to a labeled model-counting oracle?
questions.quote: The main question that our results leave open is which finite-variable fragments admit polynomial-time unlabeled model counting, rather than merely a reduction to a labeled oracle.
questions.context: The paper provides a single-query reduction from unlabeled model counting in $k$-variable logic to labeled model counting in $(k+1)$-variable logic via automorphism marking, but it does not establish which logic fragments allow computing unlabeled model counts directly in polynomial time without oracle calls.
questions.background: Familiarity with first-order model counting, counting quantifiers ($C^k$), and descriptive complexity.
questions.title: Unary Functions, Automorphisms, and Unlabeled First-Order Model Counting

questions.question: What is the exact accepting-path complexity of natural unlabeled counting functions, such as whether the sequence $(u_n)$ of nonisomorphic graphs on $n$ vertices belongs to the complexity class $\#\mathrm{P}_1$?
questions.quote: This leaves open the accepting-path complexity of many natural unlabeled counting functions.
questions.context: The paper's automorphism-marking technique yields unlabeled counts by querying a labeled oracle and dividing by $n!$, rather than explicitly selecting canonical representatives for isomorphism classes, leaving the underlying certificate/path complexity unresolved.
questions.background: Understanding of counting complexity classes like $\#\mathrm{P}$ and $\#\mathrm{P}_1$, orbit counting, and structural graph theory.
questions.title: Unary Functions, Automorphisms, and Unlabeled First-Order Model Counting

questions.question: Can the lower bound on the area of a convex universal cover for planar sets of diameter one be improved by optimizing over both the shape parameters and relative positions of irregular Reuleaux polygons (which form an $(n-3)$-parameter family at fixed $n$) rather than restricting to regular ones?
questions.quote: Irregular Reuleaux polygons form an $(n-3)$ -parameter family at fixed $n$ , and optimising over shape as well as position is a natural next question that the present method can express without modification, at a cost this paper does not attempt.
questions.context: The paper establishes a lower bound of 0.8344 on the area of any convex universal cover by analyzing placements of regular curves of constant width (disc, Reuleaux triangle, Reuleaux pentagon), but does not attempt the higher-dimensional optimization over irregular Reuleaux shapes.
questions.background: Familiarity with convex geometry, properties of curves of constant width, and interval arithmetic or spatial branch-and-bound optimization techniques.
questions.title: Curves of constant width and Lebesgue's covering problem

questions.question: How can the Context-Effect Verifier (CEV) in the LangBP framework for joint bidding and pricing be extended to incorporate online feedback under distribution shift, beyond relying on observational evidence in behavior-supported offline data?
questions.quote: CEV is limited to observational evidence in behavior-supported regions; future work could study online feedback under distribution shift.
questions.context: The paper establishes that CEV can evaluate candidate execution effects based on observational data within behavior-supported regions. However, it leaves unresolved how to update or adapt the verifier using online feedback when facing distribution shifts outside the historical behavior distribution.
questions.background: Knowledge of offline reinforcement learning, distribution shift mitigation, and online feedback optimization.
questions.title: LangBP: Language-Guided Reasoning and Acting for Joint Bidding and Pricing

questions.question: Does there exist a classical deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for factoring polynomials over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$ in large odd characteristic?
questions.quote: Whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists at all is a long-standing open problem, and a sharper statement than is sometimes made is available.
questions.context: The paper provides an exact quantum polynomial-time derandomization of the splitting step in Berlekamp's algorithm using exact amplitude amplification, but does not yield an unconditional or conditional classical deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.
questions.background: Familiarity with finite field arithmetic, Berlekamp's algorithm, and classical derandomization techniques in computer algebra.
questions.title: Exact quantum splitting and the structure of finite algebras

questions.question: Determine whether the two-parameter time--message trade-off for distributed minimum spanning tree (MST) construction in the $\textsf{CONGEST-KT}_1$ model can be improved beyond $\tilde{O}(n^{\lambda}D_G + n^{1-\kappa-\lambda} + n^{1-2\kappa+\lambda} + n^{1/2})$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(\min\{m, n^{1+\kappa}\})$ messages, and establish whether this trade-off curve is optimal.
questions.quote: Can the time–message trade-off be improved further, and is the trade-off achieved here optimal?
questions.context: The paper introduces a trade-off running in $\tilde{O}(n^{\lambda}D_G + n^{1-\kappa-\lambda} + n^{1-2\kappa+\lambda} + n^{1/2})$ rounds with $\tilde{O}(\min\{m, n^{1+\kappa}\})$ messages for any $0 \leq \lambda \leq \kappa \leq 1/2$, which breaks the existing $\tilde{\Omega}(n^2)$ product barrier, but it is unknown if this trade-off is tight.
questions.background: Familiarity with lower bounds and spanner-based graph partitioning techniques in distributed CONGEST algorithms.
questions.title: Beating Quadratic Time--Message Trade-off in Distributed Minimum Spanning Tree Construction

questions.question: Determine whether an MST algorithm in the $\textsf{CONGEST-KT}_1$ model can eliminate the multiplicative $n^{\lambda}$ factor in front of the network diameter $D_G$ to achieve an additive dependence on $D_G$ in its round complexity.
questions.quote: Can the multiplicative factor $n^{\lambda}$ ( $=\alpha$ ) that multiplies $D_{G}$ in the round complexity be removed, making the dependence on $D_{G}$ additive?
questions.context: The proposed algorithm's round complexity contains a term $n^{\lambda} D_G$, which stems from the $(\alpha, \beta)$-spanners parameter $\alpha = n^{\lambda}$, leaving open whether additive diameter dependence is possible.
questions.background: Understanding of distributed spanners, graph decomposition, and diameter-dependent round complexity bounds.
questions.title: Beating Quadratic Time--Message Trade-off in Distributed Minimum Spanning Tree Construction

questions.question: Construct message-efficient algorithms using $o(m)$ messages in the $\textsf{CONGEST-KT}_1$ model for BFS-tree construction and weighted shortest-path-tree construction.
questions.quote: Two concrete targets are BFS-tree construction and, more generally, shortest-path-tree construction on weighted graphs, for which no $o(m)$ -message algorithm is currently known in the CONGEST-KT 1 model.
questions.context: While the paper demonstrates $o(m)$-message algorithms for MST, no $o(m)$-message algorithms are known for BFS or weighted shortest-path trees in $\textsf{CONGEST-KT}_1$, despite existing in the less restrictive $\textsf{LOCAL-KT}_1$ model.
questions.background: Knowledge of distributed shortest-path structures and message-reduction techniques in the CONGEST model.
questions.title: Beating Quadratic Time--Message Trade-off in Distributed Minimum Spanning Tree Construction

questions.question: Determine whether $o(m)$ message complexity can be achieved by a deterministic algorithm for global graph problems such as MST or BFS-tree construction in the $\textsf{CONGEST-KT}_1$ model.
questions.quote: As a more general question, not necessarily tied to our approach, can $o(m)$ message complexity be attained by a deterministic algorithm?
questions.context: Existing $o(m)$-message algorithms in $\textsf{CONGEST-KT}_1$ rely on randomized strategies, whereas deterministic algorithms with $\tilde{O}(n)$ messages are only known in the $\textsf{LOCAL-KT}_1$ setting.
questions.background: Familiarity with deterministic symmetry breaking and derandomization techniques in network algorithms.
questions.title: Beating Quadratic Time--Message Trade-off in Distributed Minimum Spanning Tree Construction

questions.question: For deterministic strategy-proof mechanisms locating a new facility under a prelocated facility on a real line, determine whether the lower bound on the approximation ratio for minimizing social cost is $\Omega(n)$, closing the gap with the known $n$-approximation upper bound.
questions.quote: We conjecture the deterministic lower bound is $\Omega(n)$ just as in two-facility location games , but failed to verify it.
questions.context: The paper establishes an upper bound of $n$ and a lower bound of 1.5 for deterministic strategy-proof mechanisms under the social cost objective in the general setting on a line, leaving a wide gap between 1.5 and $n$.
questions.background: Understanding of mechanism design, strategy-proofness, and lower-bound proof techniques for facility location games on a line.
questions.title: Mechanism Design for Facility Location Games Under a Prelocated Facility

questions.question: What are the exact finite-agent bounds $\rho_{n}^{\operatorname{EFX}}$ and $\rho_{n}^{\operatorname{PMMS}}$ on the MMS guarantee of EFX and PMMS allocations for small fixed numbers of agents $n$, such as $n=3,4,5$?
questions.quote: First, while the universal and asymptotic limits are settled, determining the exact finite-agent sequences $\rho_{n}^{\operatorname{EFX}}$ $and \rho_{n}^{\operatorname{PMMS}}$ for small fixed values of $n$ (such as $n=3,4,5$ ) remains an interesting open question.
questions.context: The paper settles the universal and asymptotic limits $\rho^{\mathrm{EFX}\to\mathrm{MMS}} = \rho^{\mathrm{PMMS}\to\mathrm{MMS}} = 10/17$ for any $n$, but it leaves the exact finite-$n$ values of $\rho_{n}^{\operatorname{EFX}}$ and $\rho_{n}^{\operatorname{PMMS}}$ uncalculated for small specific values of $n$.
questions.background: Knowledge of local fairness notions (EFX and PMMS), maximin share (MMS) guarantees, and price of anarchy bounds for machine covering games.
questions.title: The Exact MMS Guarantees of EFX and PMMS

questions.question: Can the combinatorial charging schemes and bounds relating EFX/PMMS to MMS guarantees be extended beyond additive valuations to broader valuation classes, such as submodular or subadditive valuations?
questions.quote: Second, it is natural to investigate whether similar combinatorial charging schemes can be extended to broader valuation classes, such as submodular or subadditive valuations, and whether other local fairness concepts correspond to alternative game-theoretic scheduling equilibria.
questions.context: The paper establishes the exact $10/17$-MMS guarantee for EFX and PMMS strictly under nonnegative additive valuations, leaving non-additive valuation settings open for exploration.
questions.background: Familiarity with submodular and subadditive valuation functions in fair division and combinatorial charging techniques for MMS approximations.
questions.title: The Exact MMS Guarantees of EFX and PMMS

questions.question: Can the threshold packing-covering cut characterization for integer additive valuations be exploited to design pseudo-polynomial or parameterized approximation algorithms for computing the residual maximin share ($\operatorname{RMMS}$)?
questions.quote: A natural algorithmic problem is whether the threshold packing-covering characterization can be exploited to design pseudo-polynomial or parameterized approximation algorithms for computing $\operatorname{RMMS}$ .
questions.context: The paper establishes an exact threshold packing-covering cut characterization ($\operatorname{bp}_{T}(U)+\operatorname{cov}_{T}(M\setminus U)\geq n$) for integer additive valuations, but does not investigate algorithmic bounds or polynomial-time approximation schemes for computing $\operatorname{RMMS}$.
questions.background: Knowledge of parameterized algorithm design, pseudo-polynomial time algorithms, and fair division valuation models.
questions.title: Residual Maximin Share: Exact Finite-Agent Frontier, Sparse Extremizers, and Threshold Cuts

questions.question: Can alternative dynamic invariants be designed for sequential allocation mechanisms that bypass the theoretical limitation imposed by the share-based lone-divider barrier?
questions.quote: Another open direction is studying whether alternative dynamic invariants can be designed for sequential allocation mechanisms that bypass the share-based lone-divider barrier.
questions.context: The paper proves that $\operatorname{RMMS}$ is pointwise maximal among residual self-feasible shares and achieves an exact frontier of $\lambda_n=\frac{2d_n}{3d_n-1}$ (converging to $2/3$), proving a hard limitation for share-based lone-divider procedures.
questions.background: Familiarity with sequential allocation mechanisms, lone-divider procedures, and dynamic fairness invariants.
questions.title: Residual Maximin Share: Exact Finite-Agent Frontier, Sparse Extremizers, and Threshold Cuts

questions.question: Can multiple high-degree nonlinear defects interact to reduce the unrestricted Boolean XOR--AND multiplicative complexity of binary polynomial multiplication, starting with five-term binary polynomial multiplication $\operatorname{Mul}_5$?
questions.quote: Whether several such defects can interact is the next question, beginning with five-term multiplication.
questions.context: The paper proves that four-term binary polynomial multiplication $\operatorname{Mul}_4$ has unrestricted XOR--AND multiplicative complexity of exactly nine by showing that a single high-degree defect cannot expose higher Hasse jets due to jet separation and Boolean idempotence. However, determining the multiplicative complexity for five-term polynomial multiplication requires understanding whether and how multiple nonlinear defects can interact across intermediate gates.
questions.background: Requires understanding Boolean circuit lower bounds, multiplicative complexity over $\mathbb F_2$, Hasse derivatives, and the algebraic flag techniques introduced in this paper.
questions.title: Unrestricted Boolean Multiplicative Complexity of Four-Term Binary Polynomial Multiplication: Rational Places, Hasse Jets, and the Failure of Nonlinear Feedback

questions.question: Determine whether the problem of recognizing or finding a maximum-anchor map satisfying anchored list degeneracy (A-LD) for rival-injective allocations is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard.
questions.quote: We do not resolve the general complexity of finding a maximum-anchor map satisfying A-LD.
questions.context: The paper demonstrates that given a maximum-anchor map with residual support-list degeneracy, an all-good $\mathrm{EFX}_0$ allocation can be constructed in $O(nm^2)$ time by reverse greedy coloring, but leaves the general complexity of determining if such a map exists open.
questions.background: Familiarity with computational complexity theory, constraint satisfaction problems, and list coloring algorithmics.
questions.title: Rival-Injective Allocations: Support-List Structure and Maximum-Anchor EFX$_0$ Certificates

questions.question: Determine whether an all-good $\mathrm{EFX}_0$ allocation always exists for four or more agents with general additive valuations and ten or more goods.
questions.quote: Exact existence is known for three additive agents, for four additive agents with at most nine goods, and for several restricted valuation domains, but remains open for general additive valuations with four or more agents .
questions.context: The paper provides rival-injective allocation framework certificates and explicit witness families for support patterns, but these structural guarantees do not resolve unrestricted general additive $\mathrm{EFX}_0$ existence.
questions.background: Knowledge of fair division theory, additive agent valuations, and envy-freeness up to any good ($\mathrm{EFX}$).
questions.title: Rival-Injective Allocations: Support-List Structure and Maximum-Anchor EFX$_0$ Certificates

questions.question: How can the unified length-based constrained optimization framework for kirigami design be extended to accommodate kirigami structures featuring curved cuts and curved tiles?
questions.quote: In our future work, we plan to extend our work to the design of other kirigami structures involving curved cuts and curved tiles.
questions.context: The paper establishes a length-based constrained optimization framework for 2D and 3D shape-morphing kirigami structures. However, the current model only considers structures composed of straight edges and planar tiles, leaving open the formulation of constraints for non-planar tiles and curved cuts.
questions.background: Familiarity with computational geometry, discrete differential geometry, and length-based non-linear optimization techniques.
questions.title: A unified geometric design framework for kirigami structures

questions.question: Does an $\mathrm{EF1}_{\mathrm{outer}}$ allocation always exist for double sun graphs under heterogeneous monotone valuations?
questions.quote: In particular, we conjecture that our result on double suns continues to hold in this more general setting.
questions.context: The paper proves that connected $\mathrm{EF1}_{\mathrm{outer}}$ allocations exist for double suns (an infinite family of non-traceable graphs) under common monotone valuations, but leaves open whether this existence result extends to heterogeneous valuations.
questions.background: Understanding of connected fair division concepts and structural graph theory of non-traceable graphs such as double suns.
questions.title: Fair Division of Graphs: Beyond Traceability

questions.question: What is the spectrum threshold characterizing the existence of $\mathrm{EF1}_{\mathrm{outer}}$ allocations on trees under common additive valuations with two possible vertex values?
questions.quote: Beyond binary valuations, even the case of common additive valuations with only two possible vertex values remains unresolved: the threshold may differ from the binary threshold, but a natural extension of bad sets appears to be a promising candidate characterization.
questions.context: The paper characterizes the spectrum threshold for common binary additive valuations on trees using bad sets, but extending this threshold characterization to general two-value common additive valuations remains open.
questions.background: Familiarity with bad set characterizations and fair division on trees under additive valuations.
questions.title: Fair Division of Graphs: Beyond Traceability

questions.question: What is the characterization of the threshold for the existence of $\mathrm{EF1}_{\mathrm{outer}}$ allocations on general graphs beyond trees?
questions.quote: Fully characterizing the threshold beyond trees remains an important open question.
questions.context: The authors use bad sets to construct negative instances on general graphs and fully characterize the threshold for common binary additive valuations on trees, but leave the characterization for general graphs open.
questions.background: Knowledge of structural graph theory, graph connectivity, and connected item allocation mechanisms.
questions.title: Fair Division of Graphs: Beyond Traceability

questions.question: Determine whether deterministic ex ante computational hardness persists when the signal support is polynomially bounded, by either constructing a polynomial-time deterministic selector or proving a matching hardness result.
questions.quote: Therefore there is open problem whether deterministic ex ante hardness persists under polynomially bounded support; we currently have neither a polynomial-time selector nor a matching hardness result for this restricted case.
questions.context: The paper establishes that exact and signalwise Bayes-optimal selection is intractable even with small signal support, but it leaves open whether ex ante approximate performance allows polynomial-time deterministic selectors under polynomially bounded signal support.
questions.background: Familiarity with computational complexity theory, approximation algorithms, and Bayesian decision theory.
questions.title: On the Complexity of Bayesian Signal Processing

questions.question: Determine whether bounded signal support restores deterministic ex ante tractability in Bayesian signal processing, as conjectured by the author.
questions.quote: A particularly immediate open question is whether bounded signal support also restores deterministic ex ante tractability where we conjecture that it does.
questions.context: The authors show that PAC sample-based Bayesian learning is tractable if and only if signal support is bounded, but whether this bounded support condition also guarantees deterministic ex ante tractability remains open.
questions.background: Understanding of PAC learning theory, sample complexity, and Bayesian decision-making frameworks.
questions.title: On the Complexity of Bayesian Signal Processing

questions.question: Determine the performance (number of colors used) of the FirstFit ($\\FF$) online graph coloring algorithm in the random order model on bipartite graphs and $3$-colorable graphs.
questions.quote: Bosek et al already mentioned the open problem of understanding $\\FF$ ’s performance on bipartite graphs and three-colorable graphs.
questions.context: The paper demonstrates that FirstFit achieves $O(1)$ colors on crown graphs and $O(\\log n / \\log \\log n)$ on trees and cactus graphs in the random order model, while showing that high density alone is insufficient for $O(1)$ performance on general bipartite graphs. However, determining the precise competitive ratio or color count of FirstFit on general bipartite and $3$-colorable graphs under random arrival remains open.
questions.background: Requires knowledge of online graph coloring algorithms, FirstFit performance bounds, and probabilistic analysis in the random order model.
questions.title: FirstFit online coloring in the random order model

questions.question: Can non-membership in the class of scaffolding automaton (SCA) languages be derived directly from intrinsic combinatorial or information-theoretic properties of append-only scaffolds and fixed-radius access, without relying on reductions to cell-probe lower bounds?
questions.quote: It remains open whether SCA non-membership can be derived directly from combinatorial or information-theoretic properties of append-only scaffolds and fixed-radius access.
questions.context: The paper proves non-membership in SCA and PEG by transferring the execution of scaffolding automata to cell-probe data structures and invoking cell-probe lower bounds. However, this approach relies on finding a suitable data-structure reduction and does not identify intrinsic obstructions within the SCA model itself.
questions.background: Understanding of scaffolding automata (SCAs), parsing expression grammars, and lower-bound techniques in formal language theory and dynamic data structures.
questions.title: Separating Parsing Expression Grammars using Cell-Probe Lower Bounds

questions.question: What are natural necessary or sufficient conditions (or an exact characterization) for a linear context-free language to be recognized by a total parsing expression grammar (PEG), i.e., characterizing the class $\mathsf{LIN}\cap\mathsf{PEG}$?
questions.quote: Finding such a characterization, even through natural necessary or sufficient conditions for a linear context-free language to be recognized by a total PEG, remains open.
questions.context: The paper establishes that the boundary between linear context-free languages ($\mathsf{LIN}$) and PEG languages ($\mathsf{PEG}$) is nontrivial by constructing a language in $\mathsf{LIN}\setminus\mathsf{PEG}$, but it leaves open the exact structural characterization of $\mathsf{LIN}\cap\mathsf{PEG}$.
questions.background: Familiarity with context-free grammars, linear languages, and parsing expression grammars (PEGs).
questions.title: Separating Parsing Expression Grammars using Cell-Probe Lower Bounds

questions.question: Can the Plotkin-type bound derivation framework for function-correcting codes (FCCs) be extended to derive analogous redundancy bounds under distance measures outside the Wyner-Graham framework, specifically for the $b$-symbol distance and the sum-rank distance?
questions.quote: One direction of future research is to extend the approach developed in this paper to derive analogous bounds for FCCs under other distance measures, such as the $b$ -symbol distance and the sum-rank distance, which do not fall within the Wyner-Graham distance framework.
questions.context: The authors established a general Plotkin-type bound on the optimal redundancy of FCCs for distance measures belonging to the Wyner-Graham distance framework (including Hamming and Lee distances), simplifying evaluation by using preimage cardinalities and intra-preimage pairwise distances. However, distance measures such as the $b$-symbol distance and the sum-rank distance lie outside the Wyner-Graham framework and are left unaddressed.
questions.background: Familiarity with function-correcting codes, algebraic coding theory bounds, and the definitions of $b$-symbol distance and sum-rank distance.
questions.title: A General Plotkin-type Bound on Function-Correcting Codes with Wyner-Graham Distance

questions.question: Determine whether there exists a strategyproof allocation rule that guarantees an envy-free up to one item (EF1) allocation on all-normalized Boolean valuation profiles $\mathcal{V}_{1}^{n}$ for arbitrary numbers of agents $n$ and items $m$.
questions.quote: Can a strategyproof rule guarantee EF1 on $\mathcal{V}_{1}^{n}$ for arbitrary $n$ and $m$ ?
questions.context: The paper proves that for $n,m\geqslant 2$, no allocation on $\mathcal{V}_{1}^{n}$ can simultaneously satisfy Pareto optimality and EF1, ruling out mechanisms satisfying both. However, whether strategyproofness and EF1 can be achieved together without Pareto optimality on $\mathcal{V}_{1}^{n}$ remains open.
questions.background: Familiarity with strategyproof mechanism design and fair division under non-additive Boolean valuations.
questions.title: Fair Division Under Boolean Valuations: Beyond Normalization

questions.question: Identify the conditions on Boolean valuation profiles under which strategyproofness, EF1, and Pareto optimality can be satisfied simultaneously.
questions.quote: On which Boolean profiles can strategyproofness, EF1, and Pareto optimality be achieved simultaneously?
questions.context: The paper provides positive results on unnormalized profiles $\mathcal{V}_{0}^{n}$ and negative impossibility results on normalized profiles $\mathcal{V}_{1}^{n}$, but leaves mixed profiles where $0 < |Z| < n$ unclassified.
questions.background: Knowledge of Pareto efficiency, strategyproofness, and profile characterizations in fair division.
questions.title: Fair Division Under Boolean Valuations: Beyond Normalization

questions.question: Characterize the class of matroids that guarantee the existence of a matroid-feasible EF1 allocation for every Boolean valuation profile across any number of agents $n$.
questions.quote: Which matroids guarantee a feasible EF1 allocation for every Boolean profile and every number of agents?
questions.context: For $n=2$ agents, the authors prove that a feasible EF1 allocation exists if and only if the basis-pair exchange graph contains a self-complementary component, but extending this result to $n > 2$ agents requires moving beyond pairwise exchange graphs.
questions.background: Background in matroid theory, basis-pair exchange graphs, and fair division constraints.
questions.title: Fair Division Under Boolean Valuations: Beyond Normalization

questions.question: What is the computational complexity of determining the game-theoretic outcome of Domineering on standard grid graphs?
questions.quote: What is the computational complexity of Domineering ?
questions.context: The authors establish that Partizan Arc Kayles (PArcK), a generalization of Domineering to arbitrary graphs, is $\mathord{\rm PSPACE}$-complete even without green edges. However, the exact computational complexity of the original game of Domineering on grid graphs remains open.
questions.background: Knowledge of algorithmic combinatorial game theory, complexity theory, and planar graph reductions.
questions.title: It's Hard to PArcK

questions.question: What is the computational complexity of the impartial game Arc Kayles, where all edges in the game graph are green?
questions.quote: What is the computational complexity of (impartial) Arc Kayles ?
questions.context: The authors prove that Partizan Arc Kayles (PArcK) is $\mathord{\rm PSPACE}$-complete when played with partizan (red and blue) edges, but the complexity of impartial Arc Kayles (where all edges are green) remains unresolved.
questions.background: Familiarity with impartial game theory, Sprague-Grundy theory, and graph game complexity reductions.
questions.title: It's Hard to PArcK

questions.question: Can the $\Omega(1/\log K)$-approximation ratio for weighted throughput active-time scheduling with an active-time budget $K$ under unbounded capacity be improved, for instance to a constant-factor approximation?
questions.quote: The most immediate one is whether the $\Omega(1/\log K)$ -approximation for unbounded capacity can be improved.
questions.context: For general job intervals with unbounded machine capacity ($m=\infty$), the authors prove NP-hardness and rule out an FPTAS unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, while providing a pseudo-polynomial time $\Omega(1/\log K)$-approximation algorithm.
questions.background: Familiarity with approximation algorithms and LP-rounding or greedy techniques for interval scheduling and throughput maximization.
questions.title: Scheduling to Maximize Weighted Throughput with an Active-Time Budget

questions.question: Do proper or laminar interval instances of active-time scheduling to maximize weighted throughput admit exact polynomial-time algorithms, or fixed-parameter tractable algorithms parameterized by smaller parameter sets than $(K, m)$?
questions.quote: It would also be interesting to understand whether proper or laminar intervals admit polynomial-time algorithms, or fixed-parameter algorithms under smaller parameter sets.
questions.context: The authors establish a pseudo-polynomial $(nK)^{O(m)}$-time algorithm for proper intervals and an FPT algorithm parameterized jointly by $K$ and $m$ for laminar intervals, leaving open polynomial-time solvability and FPT status under individual parameters.
questions.background: Knowledge of parameterized complexity, dynamic programming on proper/laminar interval structures, and scheduling complexity.
questions.title: Scheduling to Maximize Weighted Throughput with an Active-Time Budget

questions.question: Can a direct proof of the statement in Corollary 6.6 be established purely at the level of stochastic control, without relying on the broader algorithmic machinery of the paper?
questions.quote: We do not know a proof of this fact that works purely at the level of stochastic control.
questions.context: The paper proves Corollary 6.6 by establishing the exact algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit using incremental AMP algorithms and the branching overlap gap property (OGP). However, it leaves open whether the analytical identity in Corollary 6.6 can be proven directly using stochastic control theory.
questions.background: Familiarity with stochastic control, controlled stochastic differential equations (SDEs), and high-dimensional probability.
questions.title: Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory

questions.question: Extend the convergence analysis of the proposed distributed GNE algorithms to Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problems (GNEPs) with global inequality constraints.
questions.quote: Future work includes extending the analysis to GNEPs with global inequality constraints, where formal convergence guarantees remain open, and studying how sparsity and graph structure affect communication efficiency, in particular whether $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ can be chosen sparser than $\mathcal{G}_{f}$ and what the sparsest feasible communication graph is, especially in dynamic networks where agents may join or leave.
questions.context: The authors establish convergence guarantees for fully distributed continuous-time and discrete-time algorithms solving GNEPs under shared linear equality constraints without requiring multiplier consensus, but formal convergence guarantees for GNEPs under global inequality constraints remain open.
questions.background: Requires knowledge of distributed optimization, variational inequalities, and continuous-time dynamical systems analysis for inequality-constrained non-cooperative games.
questions.title: Fully Distributed GNE Algorithms for Multi-Robot Placement without Consensus on Multipliers

questions.question: Determine whether the constraint communication graph $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ can be chosen sparser than the objective communication graph $\mathcal{G}_{f}$, and identify the sparsest feasible communication graph for distributed GNE algorithms in static and dynamic networks.
questions.quote: Future work includes extending the analysis to GNEPs with global inequality constraints, where formal convergence guarantees remain open, and studying how sparsity and graph structure affect communication efficiency, in particular whether $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ can be chosen sparser than $\mathcal{G}_{f}$ and what the sparsest feasible communication graph is, especially in dynamic networks where agents may join or leave.
questions.context: The paper utilizes two communication graphs, $\mathcal{G}_{f}$ for objective coupling and $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ for shared constraints, but leaves open the exact trade-offs between graph sparsity, connectivity, and algorithmic convergence, particularly when agents dynamically join or leave the network.
questions.background: Requires expertise in algebraic graph theory, distributed optimization algorithms, and dynamic network topology analysis.
questions.title: Fully Distributed GNE Algorithms for Multi-Robot Placement without Consensus on Multipliers

questions.question: What is the optimal randomized metric distortion for $m \geqslant 4$ candidates in metric social choice, and does its limit as $m \to \infty$ equal the asymptotic lower bound of $2.1126\ldots$?
questions.quote: For $m\geqslant 4$ candidates, determining the optimal randomized metric distortion remains open, including whether its limit as $m\to\infty$ equals the asymptotic lower bound $2.1126\ldots$ of .
questions.context: The paper establishes an upper bound of $2.3282$ on the randomized metric distortion for $m \geqslant 4$ candidates by mixing Integrated Veto with a random-size stable lottery, but a gap remains between this upper bound and the known asymptotic lower bound of $2.1126\ldots$.
questions.background: Familiarity with metric social choice, voting rules like Integrated Veto and maximal lotteries, and linear-programming duality techniques for distortion bounds.
questions.title: Improving Randomized Metric Distortion to 2.3282

questions.question: Can the techniques from the good-bad algorithm or its charging analysis be used to design simpler approximation algorithms with approximation guarantees strictly below $2$ for network-design problems such as Steiner forest and connectivity augmentation?
questions.quote: This raises the question of whether ideas from the good-bad algorithm or our charging analysis could lead to simpler algorithms with approximation guarantees below $2$ for Steiner forest, connectivity augmentation, or related problems.
questions.context: The paper establishes a simplified $3/2$-approximation proof for the good-bad algorithm on downward monotone requirement functions, but does not extend these techniques to other classical network-design problems where breaking the factor-$2$ approximation barrier is traditionally difficult.
questions.background: Understanding of approximation algorithms for network design problems, particularly primal-dual and greedy methods for Steiner forest and connectivity augmentation.
questions.title: A Simplified Analysis of the Good-Bad $3/2$-Approximation Algorithm for Some Minimum-Cost Graph Problems

questions.question: How can belief-state equilibrium search for competitive Pokémon VGC be extended to the Closed Team Sheets setting, where the opponent's unrevealed movesets, items, abilities, and stat allocations are unknown prior to the match and must be inferred during play?
questions.quote: We evaluate under Open Team Sheets and leave closed sheets, where the opponent’s unrevealed sets must be inferred, as future work.
questions.context: The paper establishes that PokaiTrainer can achieve competitive performance (settling in a 1350–1400 Elo band) under Open Team Sheets, where both players have full knowledge of each other's team configurations. It leaves open how to perform search when opponent sets are hidden at the start of the game, requiring online probabilistic belief updates over unrevealed team configurations.
questions.background: Familiarity with imperfect-information game theory, Bayesian belief state inference, and equilibrium search algorithms such as Student of Games.
questions.title: PokaiTrainer: Scaling Belief-State Search to Competitive Pokémon VGC

questions.question: Can the approximation gap for Ulam median and Ulam center rank aggregation be narrowed by improving the $51/50-\varepsilon$ NP-hardness lower bound or developing better polynomial-time approximation algorithms?
questions.quote: A natural next step is to narrow the substantial gap between these lower bounds and the best known approximation algorithms.
questions.context: The paper proves a factor $51/50-\varepsilon$ NP-hardness of approximation for both Ulam median and center even with four input permutations, leaving a large quantitative gap between this lower bound and existing upper bounds.
questions.background: Requires knowledge of approximation algorithms for metric rank aggregation and techniques for proving hardness of approximation.
questions.title: Hardness of Approximation of Rank Aggregation on Ulam Metric

questions.question: Can stronger inapproximability lower bounds be proven for Ulam median or Ulam center when the number of input permutations is arbitrary rather than fixed to four?
questions.quote: It would be especially interesting to obtain stronger hardness of approximation even for an arbitrary number of inputs, or to identify additional structure that can be exploited algorithmically.
questions.context: The authors establish NP-hardness of approximation within factor $51/50-\varepsilon$ using instances of size four, but have not ruled out larger constant or non-constant hardness factors when the input contains an arbitrary number of permutations.
questions.background: Requires experience in hardness of approximation reductions, probabilistically checkable proofs, and edit/Ulam distance properties.
questions.title: Hardness of Approximation of Rank Aggregation on Ulam Metric

questions.question: Is it possible to achieve an approximation algorithm for the Ulam center problem with an approximation ratio strictly less than $2$ when the number of input permutations is part of the input?
questions.quote: For Ulam center, determining whether one can beat factor $2$ when the number of inputs is part of the input remains another compelling open direction.
questions.context: Standard metric center properties yield a factor-$2$ approximation algorithm, while the paper proves NP-hardness up to factor $51/50-\varepsilon$; it remains unknown whether a factor strictly better than $2$ is achievable in polynomial time for arbitrary instance sizes.
questions.background: Requires familiarity with approximation algorithms for metric center problems and alignment algorithm techniques for the Ulam metric.
questions.title: Hardness of Approximation of Rank Aggregation on Ulam Metric

questions.question: What is the exact core approximation ratio for proportionally fair clustering in the general setting where candidate center locations $C$ do not necessarily contain all agent locations $N$?
questions.quote: Resolving the gap in the general setting appears to be the largest theoretical open problem remaining in the study of the core in clustering.
questions.context: The paper settles the optimal core approximation bound of $2$ for the special case where $N \subseteq C$, but leaves open the tight approximation factor for the general case where candidate locations may be restricted.
questions.background: Understanding of fair metric clustering, core concepts from computational social choice, and Scarf's theorem for non-transferable utility games.
questions.title: Optimally Selecting Representative Agents from a Metric Space

questions.question: Does the Borda count voting rule admit a constant-competitive preference elicitation algorithm under the next-best query model, or must every algorithm have a competitive ratio that grows with the number of alternatives $m$?
questions.quote: Open Question: Does Borda admit a constant-competitive elicitation algorithm?
questions.context: The paper develops active preference elicitation algorithms for positional scoring rules and establishes an $O(\sqrt{m})$ competitive ratio upper bound for Borda count using multi-scale score thresholding, but leaves open whether an optimal competitive ratio of $O(1)$ is achievable.
questions.background: Familiarity with competitive analysis of online active algorithms, positional scoring rules, and preference elicitation in social choice theory.
questions.title: The Art of Calling the Winner by Asking Just Enough Questions: Competitive Preference Elicitation with Next-Best Queries

questions.question: Can competitive active preference elicitation algorithms under next-best queries be developed for alternative targets such as achieving a desired distortion guarantee or fairness notions like proportional fairness or justified representation?
questions.quote: In this paper, the target was winner determination under popular voting rules, but future work can replace this by a desired distortion guarantee or a desired level of fairness, e.g., proportional fairness or justified representation .
questions.context: The paper focuses strictly on exact winner determination under standard voting rules; it leaves unexplored how to perform active preference elicitation to approximate optimal social welfare (distortion) or satisfy axiomatic fairness guarantees.
questions.background: Understanding of distortion bounds in computational social choice and multi-winner fairness concepts such as proportional fairness and justified representation.
questions.title: The Art of Calling the Winner by Asking Just Enough Questions: Competitive Preference Elicitation with Next-Best Queries

questions.question: Is the minimax competitive ratio for online shoreline search in two dimensions, $C^{*}_{2}$, equal to the stationary spiral ratio $C_{2,\mathrm{stat}}$?
questions.quote: The equality $C^{*}_{2}=C_{2,\mathrm{stat}}$ remains open.
questions.context: The paper identifies the stationary relative equilibrium in $D=2$ as a logarithmic spiral whose pitch is selected by bottleneck chord tangency, but it does not establish whether non-stationary strategies could yield a lower competitive ratio.
questions.background: Requires familiarity with online search theory, competitive analysis, logarithmic spirals, and continuous Bellman equations.
questions.title: Bellman--Shoreline Search in Arbitrary Dimension: Exponential Vector Oscillators, Active Memory, Precession, and Effective Computability

questions.question: What is the complete global classification of discounted bottleneck faces for exponential search orbits across arbitrary finite dimensions?
questions.quote: Canonical tower faces are explicit; the global classification of discounted bottleneck faces remains open.
questions.context: The paper provides explicit canonical faces for the harmonic tower subclass in both even and odd dimensions, but leaves open the classification of discounted bottleneck faces in the absence of harmonic assumptions.
questions.background: Requires expertise in convex analysis, support functions, log-directional geometry, and hyperspherical parametrizations.
questions.title: Bellman--Shoreline Search in Arbitrary Dimension: Exponential Vector Oscillators, Active Memory, Precession, and Effective Computability

questions.question: Can profitable storage-and-handoff cycles be ruled out to show that the minimax shoreline search problem ultimately selects a precessing orbit class?
questions.quote: The stronger structural problem remains: rule out profitable storage-and-handoff cycles, understand switches, and determine whether the minimax problem ultimately selects a particular precessing class.
questions.context: The paper proves local envelope laws, tangent conditions, delay identities, and general computability, but does not prove global stationarity or reduce the functional Bellman state space to a finite state.
questions.background: Requires background in dynamic programming, delay differential systems, minimax optimization, and continuous online search.
questions.title: Bellman--Shoreline Search in Arbitrary Dimension: Exponential Vector Oscillators, Active Memory, Precession, and Effective Computability

questions.question: Determine whether the optimal deterministic planar Shoreline search competitive ratio $C_2^*$ is realized by a search trajectory in the logarithmic spiral regime.
questions.quote: The next challenge is not to prove that the value exists as a computable object, but to make certificates small enough to yield new numerical bounds and to determine whether the spiral regime actually realizes that value.
questions.context: The paper establishes that the optimal value $C_2^*$ for deterministic planar Shoreline search is a computable real number via finite self-similar cell reductions and quantifier elimination, but it leaves open whether an optimal trajectory actually belongs to the logarithmic spiral regime.
questions.background: Understanding of planar shoreline search problems, Bellman search dynamics, and relative equilibria of logarithmic spirals.
questions.title: Bellman Search in Arbitrary Finite Dimension: A Self-Similar Cell Theorem and Effective Computability of Planar Shoreline Search

questions.question: Construct sufficiently small computational certificates for planar Shoreline search to obtain explicit numerical bounds on $C_2^*$.
questions.quote: The next challenge is not to prove that the value exists as a computable object, but to make certificates small enough to yield new numerical bounds and to determine whether the spiral regime actually realizes that value.
questions.context: The paper provides a theoretical algorithm proving that $C_2^*$ is computable to within any arbitrary rational precision $\varepsilon > 0$, but the bounds from quantifier elimination and polygonal cell coding are too large to yield practical numerical bounds.
questions.background: Experience with real algebraic geometry, quantifier elimination algorithms, and certified geometric optimization.
questions.title: Bellman Search in Arbitrary Finite Dimension: A Self-Similar Cell Theorem and Effective Computability of Planar Shoreline Search

questions.question: Prove analytically that the defender's upper and lower payoff bounds coincide for general $n$ attack types in the networked multi-resource General Lotto game.
questions.quote: For general $n$ , we leave open the problem of proving analytically that our upper and lower bounds are equal.
questions.context: The paper establishes upper and lower bounds on the defender's performance in a networked multi-resource General Lotto game and analytically proves that the bounds coincide for $n = 2$ attack types, while offering numerical evidence of tightness for general $n$.
questions.background: Familiarity with game theory, multi-resource Colonel Lotto games, continuous zero-sum games, and linear programming duality.
questions.title: Networked Multi-Resource Defense Capabilities in a General Lotto Game

questions.question: Prove that quadratic probing achieves an $O(1)$ expected insertion time when the hash table is at a 50% load factor.
questions.quote: Even proving an $O(1)$ expected-time bound for a table that is 50% full remains open.
questions.context: This paper establishes an expected insertion time of $\varepsilon^{-(1+o(1))}$ at load factor $1 - \varepsilon$, but proving a strict $O(1)$ expected time bound for a constant load factor such as $50\%$ remains open.
questions.background: Familiarity with open-address hash tables, quadratic probing, and probabilistic analysis of data structures.
questions.title: Quadratic Probing Insertions Are $ε^{-(1+o(1))}$

questions.question: Determine whether witness tree and witness forest proof techniques can be extended to analyze open-address hashing schemes at higher load factors.
questions.quote: Whether or not these types of witness tree/forest arguments can be extended to higher load factors remains an interesting open question.
questions.context: Prior work uses witness tree/forest arguments to analyze probing and hashing schemes, but these techniques have traditionally been limited to lower load factors.
questions.background: Knowledge of witness tree and witness forest arguments used in analyzing randomized data structures.
questions.title: Quadratic Probing Insertions Are $ε^{-(1+o(1))}$

questions.question: Can randomized online algorithms achieve a strictly smaller competitive ratio than the $\Theta(\log M)$ bound achieved by deterministic algorithms for classical memory allocation without request fragmentation?
questions.quote: Interestingly, it has remained an open question whether randomized algorithms might be able to beat deterministic ones.
questions.context: In classical memory allocation without request fragmentation, the optimal competitive ratio for deterministic online allocators is $\Theta(\log M)$, where $M$ is the volume high-water mark of the underlying request sequence. It remains open whether randomized online allocators can achieve a strictly better competitive ratio in this unfragmented setting.
questions.background: Familiarity with online algorithms, competitive analysis, and randomized lower bound techniques for memory allocation.
questions.title: Tight Bounds for Memory Allocation With and Without Request Fragmentation

questions.question: Is the combinatorial discrepancy $\mathsf{disc}(A) := \min_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} \|Ax\|_\infty$ of every matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ whose columns have Euclidean norm at most one bounded by a universal constant $O(1)$?
questions.quote: A central open problem in discrepancy theory is a conjecture of Komlós from the 1980s which asserts that $\mathsf{disc}(A)$ is bounded by a universal constant whenever every column of $A$ has Euclidean norm at most one.
questions.context: The paper proves an upper bound of $O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})$ on the combinatorial discrepancy for matrices with column Euclidean norm at most one, improving upon Banaszczyk's $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ bound, but leaving open whether the true bound is $O(1)$.
questions.background: Familiarity with combinatorial discrepancy theory, convex geometry, vector balancing techniques, and high-dimensional probability.
questions.title: An Exposition of the $\widetilde{O}(\log^{1/4} n)$ Bound for the Komlós Problem

questions.question: For fixed constant $k$, can an approximation algorithm for $k$-tier Flexible Graph Connectivity ($k$-tier FGC) be designed with an approximation ratio depending only on the tier requirements $q_1, \dots, q_k$ (and independent of $n$), and can the paper's LP relaxation achieve this bound?
questions.quote: The most pressing open question is whether the dependence on $k$ and $n$ in the approximation factor of Theorem 1.1 can be reduced or eliminated in exchange for a dependence on tier requirements.
questions.context: The authors introduce the $k$-tier Flexible Graph Connectivity problem and give an LP-based logarithmic approximation algorithm with factor $O(k^2 \log n)$, proving that the integrality gap of their LP relaxation is between $2k$ and $O(k^2 \log n)$. They leave open whether the $n$-dependence in the approximation guarantee can be removed to yield an approximation factor depending only on the tier requirements.
questions.background: Techniques in network design approximation algorithms, specifically linear programming relaxations, iterative rounding, and multiobjective cut properties.
questions.title: Multi-tier Flexible Graph Connectivity

questions.question: Can one obtain a polylogarithmic approximation algorithm for the general version of the connected $k$-median problem while opening exactly $k$ centers?
questions.quote: The most natural question is whether one can obtain polylogarithmic approximation guarantees for the general version containing exactly $k$ centers.
questions.context: The authors give an $O(\log^2 n)$-approximation for the assignment version, but for the general version of connected $k$-median, their algorithm is bicriteria, opening $O(k \log n)$ centers to achieve an $O(\log^2 n)$-approximation in cost. It remains open whether the center budget violation can be eliminated.
questions.background: Knowledge of configuration LPs, LP rounding for $k$-median, and connectivity constraints in graph algorithms.
questions.title: A Configuration-LP Framework for Connected $k$-Median Clustering

questions.question: Can one design rooted minimum-density connected set oracles with approximation ratios strictly better than $O(\log n)$ on restricted graph families such as minor-closed graphs?
questions.quote: Another promising direction is to design stronger rooted minimum-density oracles for restricted graph families, such as minor-closed graphs.
questions.context: The proposed framework reduces the connected $k$-median problem to a covering LP coupled with a rooted minimum-density oracle; while general graphs admit an $O(\log n)$-approximation oracle, structured graph families currently lack improved bounds.
questions.background: Familiarity with structural graph theory (e.g., minor-closed graphs) and density-based connectivity approximation algorithms.
questions.title: A Configuration-LP Framework for Connected $k$-Median Clustering

questions.question: Can one construct an efficient online differentially private (DP) algorithm for $k$-means and $k$-median clustering that achieves a tight additive error dependency on the number of clusters $k$, matching bounds known in the offline setting?
questions.quote: More generally, while efficient DP algorithms with tight additive errors in terms of $k$ are known in the offline setting , none is known for the online setting.
questions.context: The paper achieves a nearly optimal additive error dependency on dimension $d$, but its additive error dependency on $k$ is sub-optimal due to DP composition across multiple sequential runs of the private dense ball subroutine.
questions.background: Requires familiarity with differentially private clustering, DP composition techniques, and online or streaming dense ball algorithms.
questions.title: Online Differentially Private Consistent Clustering

questions.question: Is it possible to construct an online differentially private (DP) coreset (achieving zero additive multiplicative error $\eta_{1}=0$) rather than a semi-coreset for online $k$-means/$k$-median clustering?
questions.quote: Our online construction (and that of ) only yields a semi-coreset, which naturally leaves the question of whether an online DP coreset construction (i.e., obtaining $\eta_{1}=0$ in Definition 4 ) is possible.
questions.context: The authors present a generic reduction that transforms a private input stream into a privatized semi-coreset, leaving open whether exact online DP coresets with zero additive multiplicative error can be obtained.
questions.background: Requires knowledge of streaming coreset constructions, differential privacy, and geometric summarization.
questions.title: Online Differentially Private Consistent Clustering

questions.question: Can the utility guarantees of the proposed online DP consistent clustering framework (and non-private Meyerson's sketch) be proven in an adversarial streaming model where the adversary observes previous outputs before selecting the next item?
questions.quote: While our privacy analysis holds for the adversarial setting (where the adversary sees outputs up to time $i-1$ before selecting $x_{i}$ ), our current utility analysis assumes an oblivious data stream.
questions.context: The paper's differential privacy analysis holds against an adaptive adversary, but the utility analysis for $k$-means and $k$-median clustering explicitly relies on an oblivious stream assumption.
questions.background: Requires an understanding of adaptive/adversarial streaming models, differential privacy, and utility analysis of online clustering algorithms.
questions.title: Online Differentially Private Consistent Clustering

questions.question: Can the polynomial dependency on $k$ and $d$ in the overhead factor $\Lambda$ of the online DP clustering reduction be improved to nearly linear time in $k$?
questions.quote: It remains an interesting question whether this can be sped up further, e.g., to nearly linear time in $k$ .
questions.context: The overall stream processing running time is $n^{1+o(1)}$ for $k,d \le n^{o(1)}$, but the polynomial factor in $k$ and $d$ comes from using a 1-Cluster algorithm as a black box inside the private Meyerson's sketch reduction.
